cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
We've followed charge through electric circuits.
Now we ask what a current does to the space around it.
A steady current creates a magnetic field, represented by the vector B.
Its SI unit is the tesla.
A straight wire produces field lines that circle the wire, not lines that
point
along it.
Use your right hand: point your thumb along conventional current, and your
curled fingers give the magnetic field direction.
Conventional current is opposite electron drift in a metal, so use the current
arrow printed in the question.
Imagine a vertical wire carrying current upward on the page.
To its right, the magnetic field points into the page.
To its left, it points out.
We represent a vector coming toward you by a dot, like an arrow tip, and one
going away by a cross, like the tail of an arrow.
Reverse the current and the field reverses.
These symbols describe a direction perpendicular to the page; they do not mean
a positive or negative field magnitude.
Also, do not confuse the direction of magnetic field with the direction of
magnetic force on a moving charge.
The force requires another vector rule that we will study separately.
Our first job is to find B at a chosen observation point.
We will use steady currents and thin wire models in vacuum or approximately
air, and state the geometry before applying a formula.
The Biot Savart law connects a small piece of current carrying wire to its
contribution at an observation point.
Draw a tiny directed length, d l, along conventional current.
Draw the displacement from that piece to the observation point; its magnitude
is r.
The small field magnitude is mu zero over four pi, multiplied by current,
directed length magnitude and sine theta, then divided by r squared.
Theta is the angle between the current element and that displacement.
The direction follows d l crossed with the unit displacement vector, using the
right hand cross product rule.
A perpendicular displacement gives the largest contribution for the same
current, length and distance.
Along the element's direction, sine theta is zero.
To obtain the field of a whole wire, add the vector contributions by
integration; don't substitute the total wire length into a small element
expression when distance or angle changes.
For an approximate tiny segment example, use four amperes, length one
centimeter, perpendicular distance ten centimeters.
Treat distance and angle as nearly constant across that short piece.
With mu zero over four pi approximately ten to the minus seven, its
contribution is four times ten to the minus seven tesla, or zero point four
microtesla.
That is the contribution of this piece, not a complete wire or its return
path.
In standard JEE numericals we use mu zero approximately four pi times ten to
the minus seven tesla meter per ampere.
Geometry and vector direction must accompany the arithmetic.
For a straight wire, integration gives a useful result.
At perpendicular distance a from a wire that is effectively very long in both
directions, the field magnitude is mu zero I divided by two pi a.
Field strength falls as one over distance, even though a single small element
contribution contains one over r squared.
Integration changes the dependence.
A five ampere long wire produces twenty microtesla at five centimeters.
Double the distance and the field becomes ten microtesla.
Now keep the wire finite.
If the perpendicular from the observation point meets the segment between its
endpoints, define alpha and beta as the positive angles from that
perpendicular
toward the two endpoint lines.
The field is mu zero I divided by four pi a, multiplied by sine alpha plus
sine
beta.
A symmetric segment with both angles forty five degrees, at the same five
centimeters and five amperes, gives ten times square root two microtesla,
about
fourteen point one four.
This is smaller than the infinite wire result because there is less
contributing wire.
Let both angles approach ninety degrees and the long wire result returns.
If the perpendicular foot lies outside the segment, use signed endpoint
geometry or rederive the integral rather than adding two positive sines
blindly.
The formula gives magnitude; use the current direction to determine into or
out
of the page.
Nearby return wires can also contribute, so read the complete circuit
geometry.
A circular loop has a different symmetry.
At its center, every current element is perpendicular to the displacement
toward the center, and each is the same distance R away.
All field contributions point along the loop axis.
Integrating around the circumference gives mu zero I divided by two R.
For N closely wound identical turns carrying the same current, multiply by N,
provided their radii and positions are approximately the same.
Curl your right fingers along the loop current; your thumb gives the central
field direction.
Counterclockwise current as viewed on the page gives field out of the page at
the center.
For a single loop of radius ten centimeters carrying four amperes, the center
field is eight pi microtesla, approximately twenty five point one three.
Along the axis at distance x from the center, contributions have transverse
components that cancel in opposite pairs.
Their axial components add.
The result is mu zero N I R squared divided by twice the quantity R squared
plus x squared raised to three halves.
Set x equal to zero and the center formula returns.
Set x equal to R and the field is the center value divided by two square root
two, here about eight point eight nine microtesla.
This equation is for points on the axis, not arbitrary points in the plane of
the loop.
State whether a question asks for the center, an axial point or another
geometry before choosing the expression.
Let's finish with two common JEE patterns.
For a circular arc, the center field contribution is proportional to the angle
swept out.
The magnitude is mu zero I times theta divided by four pi R, with theta
in radians.
A semicircle has theta equal to pi, so its contribution is half that of a full
loop with the same radius and current.
Our four ampere, ten centimeter semicircular arc contributes four pi
microtesla, about twelve point five seven.
Its direction still follows the current around the arc.
Straight leads directed radially toward or away from that center contribute
zero there, because their current elements and displacement vectors are
parallel.
This is a geometry statement, not a rule that all connecting leads have zero
field.
Include other lead contributions when needed.
Now place two very long parallel wires ten centimeters apart, each carrying
five amperes upward.
At the midpoint, each gives twenty microtesla, but one field enters the page
and the other leaves, so they cancel.
Reverse the current in one wire and both midpoint fields point the same way,
giving forty microtesla.
Notice that these are field comparisons, not statements about forces between
the wires.
For your final checklist, identify the observation point, convert distances,
choose a formula with matching geometry, establish every direction, and then
add vectors.
Ampere's law will give us another powerful way to use symmetry in the next
class.
